design_detail: Single-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-arm randomized trial (1:1) in an outpatient research clinic of the San Francisco Department of Public Health, August 2013 to September/October 2017; a larger and longer replication of Colfax et al. (2011) by an overlapping team. 120 cisgender men (115) and transgender women (5) who have sex with men, with SCID-diagnosed methamphetamine dependence and a methamphetamine-positive urine, received mirtazapine (15 mg for 1 week, then 30 mg daily) or matched placebo for 24 weeks, then 12 weeks of follow-up off medication, with weekly 30-minute counselling (CBT and motivational interviewing) and weekly urine tests. Primary analysis: GEE log-link model of piecewise linear trends in weekly urine positivity (week 1 omitted), with treatment effects at 12, 24 and 36 weeks. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835.
can_establish: Whether, in this population receiving weekly counselling, mirtazapine reduced the modelled rate of methamphetamine-positive weekly urines over 12 and 24 weeks of treatment and 12 weeks after stopping, and how often mirtazapine produced short-term abstinence compared with placebo.
cannot_establish: That mirtazapine produces abstinence (abstinence outcomes were not significantly different and most participants never achieved sustained abstinence); whether the effect holds outside cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men, in people with depression or psychotic disorders, or with better adherence; or that the self-reported sexual-behaviour changes reduce HIV transmission (not measured). Nor can it serve as independent replication of the 2011 trial, which came from the same team, site, design and analysis model.

sample.recruitment: Community recruitment through clinics, community-based organizations, nightlife venues and websites; telephone pre-screen, two screening visits and two run-in visits (with urine collection) to test retention before enrolment. Participants could receive up to 595 dollars for study visits (Methods › Recruitment; Procedures).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included (per the paper): age 18 to 65; SCID-diagnosed DSM-IV-TR methamphetamine dependence; interest in reducing or stopping use; assigned male at birth (any gender identity) or assigned female at birth and identifying as male; anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months; methamphetamine-positive urine; for people with HIV, CD4 above 200 or 100 to 199 with viral load below 200 copies/mL. Excluded: prior mirtazapine trial; mirtazapine, MAO inhibitors or antidepressants in the past 30 days except five named SSRIs; current major depression or any psychiatric condition precluding safe participation; liver tests above 5 times the upper limit; eGFR below 40; pending legal proceedings with high risk of incarceration; other research participation.
sample.demographics: Mean age 43.3 (SD 9.8); 50.8% White, 25.8% African American, 12.5% Latinx; 115 cisgender men and 5 transgender women (1 mirtazapine, 4 placebo); 51.7% HIV-positive; 68.3% not employed; 56.7% with income below 20,000 dollars. Methamphetamine use 5 to 7 days a week in 51.7%, 2 to 4 days in 30.8%, at most 1 day in 17.5% (23.3% placebo vs 11.7% mirtazapine); routes: smoked 84.2%, snorted 38.3%, injected 40.8%, rectal 27.5%, oral 16.7%. Mean CES-D 20.2 (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout 20 of 60 (33%) on mirtazapine and 13 of 60 (22%) on placebo (P = .21); final (week 36) visit completed by 38 and 42. Mean weekly visit completion 66% (69% vs 63%). Urine samples were missing for 34%, 41% and 36% of participants at weeks 12, 24 and 36, against 10%, 15% and 20% assumed in the power calculation (Results › Retention and adherence; Methamphetamine use).
sample.selection_effects: Of 241 assessed, 120 were enrolled; the commonest exclusions were psychotic disorder (40), absence of methamphetamine dependence (18), no positive urine (10), inability to adhere to procedures (8) and excluded antidepressants (5). Run-in visits selected people able to attend. The population is restricted to people who have sex with men, without major depression or psychotic disorders, and paid for attendance.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study medication: mirtazapine or identical over-encapsulated placebo prepared off site; 15 mg (or placebo) in week 1, then 30 mg daily to week 24; dispensed at baseline, weekly for 2 weeks, then every 4 weeks in WisePill electronic dispensers. Adherence by WisePill events and by self-report.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as above (oral, daily, 24 weeks, then 12 weeks without medication). WisePill adherence: weeks 2 to 12, 38.5% (SD 27.0) mirtazapine vs 39.5% (26.2) placebo; weeks 13 to 24, 28.1% (23.4) vs 38.5% (27.0) as printed; at least 50% adherence in 37% vs 35% (week 12) and 22% vs 20% (week 24).
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use was assessed weekly by audio computer-assisted self-interview but is not reported; one participant on mirtazapine died of an unintentional opioid overdose. Four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs, with no association with urine results.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: participants were actively using (80% urine-positive at baseline: 85% mirtazapine, 75% placebo) and the outcome is urine positivity during and after treatment.

comparison.controls: Matched placebo on the same schedule, with the same weekly counselling, HIV risk-reduction counselling and visit payments.
comparison.matching: 1:1 sequence generated by the study biostatistician; allocation known only to the off-site biostatistician and pharmacist; block size not stated. Baseline differences: methamphetamine-positive urine 85% vs 75% (P = .16); craving 5.8 vs 4.7 (P = .08); use on at most 1 day a week 11.7% vs 23.3%; high school or less 30.0% vs 45.0%; full-time employment 18.3% vs 8.3%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same population; not reported for either arm.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: weekly methamphetamine-metabolite urine test (MedTox EZ-Screen, qualitative), analysed as a repeated binary indicator over weeks 2 to 12, 13 to 24 and 25 to 36. Secondary: six self-reported sexual-risk measures by audio computer-assisted self-interview (past 4 weeks). Also craving, Severity of Dependence Scale, Athens Insomnia Scale, sleep hours, CES-D, adherence, adverse events, end-of-study abstinence (no methamphetamine in the last 2 weeks of each evaluation period) and 'beyond-threshold weeks of success'.
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine testing is objective but qualitative and covers only recent use; abstinence measures are urine-defined. Sexual-risk outcomes are self-reported counts.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit is a greater decline in the modelled probability of a positive weekly urine on mirtazapine than on placebo, after accounting for the fitted baseline difference, expressed as relative risks at 12 weeks and as 'net' relative risks at 24 and 36 weeks.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors acknowledge a large number of secondary outcomes at multiple time points without adjustment. 33 counts 3 primary time points, 18 sexual-behaviour estimates (6 measures at 3 time points), 6 sleep and depression estimates, 3 end-of-study abstinence comparisons and 3 beyond-threshold comparisons; adherence, craving, dependence-severity and as-treated comparisons come on top.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind (registry: participant, investigator and outcomes assessor masked). At week 24, 46% on mirtazapine and 49% on placebo guessed their assignment correctly (P = .83), although fatigue or drowsiness was reported by 30% on mirtazapine and 10% on placebo.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary (intention-to-treat GEE, robust SEs): RR for a positive urine 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.87), P = .003, at 12 weeks; 'net' RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00), P = .05, at 24 weeks; 'net' RR 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96), P = .02, at 36 weeks (12 weeks after stopping). Raw positivity among samples provided: week 12, 25 of 38 (66%) vs 32 of 41 (78%); week 24, 20 of 32 (63%) vs 29 of 39 (74%); week 36, 25 of 35 (71%) vs 37 of 42 (88%). Editors' calculation from these counts (cross-sectional, ignoring the baseline difference and missing samples): risk differences -12.3 (95% CI -32.0 to 7.4), -11.9 (-33.5 to 9.8) and -16.7 (-34.6 to 1.2) percentage points. End-of-study abstinence (last 2 weeks): 11 (18%) vs 5 (8%) at weeks 12 and 24 (OR 2.50, 0.80 to 7.61; P = .11), 7 (12%) vs 3 (5%) at week 36 (OR 2.50, 0.62 to 10.20; P = .19); reported numbers needed to treat 10, 10 and 15; editors' risk difference at week 12, 10.0 points (-2.0 to 22.0). Beyond-threshold weeks of success: median 0 (IQR 0 to 0) in both arms at all time points. As-treated (upper half of adherence): cumulative adherence RR 0.70 (0.38 to 1.28) at 12 weeks and 0.69 (0.50 to 0.95) at 24 weeks; past-week adherence 0.64 (0.36 to 1.13) and 0.73 (0.50 to 1.08). Sexual risk at 24 weeks: male partners RR 0.52 (0.27 to 0.97); condomless anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.47 (0.23 to 0.97); condomless receptive anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.37 (0.14 to 0.93); all P = .04; three other measures not significant; no differences at 12 or 36 weeks. CES-D net -6.18 (-11.07 to -1.30) at 24 weeks only; Athens Insomnia Scale -1.40 (-2.74 to -0.07) at 24 weeks only.
analysis.covariates: None in the primary model beyond the fitted baseline difference; a sensitivity model adjusted for imbalanced baseline characteristics and baseline correlates of missing or positive urines.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835, first submitted 25 June 2013 and posted 28 June 2013, before the August 2013 start. The registered primary outcome (number of methamphetamine-positive urine tests, efficacy at 12 and 24 weeks of treatment and whether sustained to week 36) and secondary outcome (sexual risk: male partners, partners with whom methamphetamine was used, unprotected anal sex with serodiscordant partners) are unchanged since registration and match the paper; adherence and adverse events are registered as other outcomes. Depression, insomnia and abstinence-based outcomes are not registered. Registry eligibility differs from the paper's (age 18 to 69 vs 18 to 65; anal sex within 3 vs 6 months; all antidepressants excluded vs five SSRIs allowed; bipolar or psychotic disorder excluded). No results are posted on the registry. The protocol is in a supplement that was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity-analysis estimates (week 1 included, missing imputed positive, adjusted, out-of-window visits, stratified by use intensity) are given only qualitatively in the text, with numbers in an unread supplementary table; stratification by baseline use intensity showed no significant effect. Other substance use and self-reported methamphetamine use are not reported.
analysis.power: 80% power for RRs of 0.81 (weeks 2 to 12), 0.86 (13 to 24) and 0.85 (25 to 36), assuming 90%, 85% and 80% retention and within-person correlation of 0.45. Observed missing urine rates (34% to 41%) were well above the assumed 10% to 20%; the authors state minimum detectable effects were nonetheless similar.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Modelled urine positivity fell more on mirtazapine (RR 0.67 at 12 weeks; 0.75 at 24 weeks, upper limit 1.00; 0.73 at 36 weeks). In absolute terms most samples stayed positive in both arms (63% to 71% on mirtazapine, 74% to 88% on placebo at weeks 12 to 36), the mirtazapine arm started with more positive urines (85% vs 75%), a third or more of samples were missing at each assessment, and abstinence did not differ significantly (18% vs 8% end-of-study abstinence; median 0 weeks of sustained success in both arms). Adherence was below 40% in both arms. Sexual-risk differences appeared only at 24 weeks, for 3 of 6 measures at P = .04, without multiplicity correction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points state that mirtazapine is the first medication to show efficacy for methamphetamine use disorder in 2 independent randomized trials and that the sexual-risk findings were consistent with the earlier study; the abstract concludes that mirtazapine reduced methamphetamine use and some HIV risk behaviours with benefits lasting after treatment. The two trials share investigators, site, population and analysis model, so 'independent' is overstated; the earlier trial found sexual-risk reductions at 12 weeks, this one found none at 12 weeks. The Discussion is more measured, calling the reduction modest overall and non-significant on abstinence-based analyses, and the Limitations note the unadjusted multiple secondary comparisons.

timeline.event: Colfax et al.: 12-week trial in 60 MSM at the same health department (RR 0.57 for a positive urine at 12 weeks); this trial is its planned expansion.
This trial: 120 participants, 24 weeks of treatment plus 12 weeks of follow-up; direction of the urine effect reproduced (RR 0.67 at 12 weeks).
Siefried et al. systematic review (search to June 2019) describes this trial in its Discussion as a replication but does not include it among its 43 trials.

replication.where_it_stands: Two trials from one team, one site and one population show the same direction of effect on urine positivity with the same analysis model; the effect on abstinence is not significant in either. Replication by an independent group, in other populations and with abstinence or use-days outcomes, had not been identified in this reading.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grant R01DA034527 and National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01DA031678; the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author has led NIH-funded studies receiving donated ledipasvir-sofosbuvir from Gilead Sciences (2016 to 2017), outside this work, and has received grant or contract support from NIH, CDC, SAMHSA, AHRQ and UCSF; the other authors report grant or contract support from public and foundation funders (NIH, CDC, HIV Prevention Trials Network, MPact Global Action, DARPA, PCORI, Alzheimer's Foundation, American Cancer Society, Buffett Foundation, Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs); one reports NIDA grants during the conduct of the study.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the San Francisco Department of Public Health and the University of California San Francisco. Five authors (G-M Santos, Vittinghoff, Matheson, D Santos, Colfax) were authors of the 2011 trial this study replicates; the co-first authors had full access to the data. No industry funding of this trial is reported. Second reading: the funding and conflict-of-interest details on this card could not be re-checked, because the saved page used for the second reading has no Article Information block; treat the funder, the disclosures and the role-of-funder statement as single-reader.

what_would_settle_it: An independent multi-site placebo-controlled trial of mirtazapine in a broader population of people with methamphetamine use disorder (including women, heterosexual men and people with depression), with a registered primary outcome on urine-verified use days or abstinence, strategies that keep missing urine data low, verified adherence, follow-up of at least 6 months after stopping, and HIV or STI incidence if the prevention claim is to be tested.

domains.note: Statistician-generated sequence with allocation held off site by the biostatistician and pharmacist and identical over-encapsulation; baseline differences (85% vs 75% positive urine; craving; frequency of use) are compatible with chance, though the primary-outcome imbalance matters for a model that estimates divergence from baseline.
Double-blind with an intention-to-treat analysis; similar (low) adherence in both arms; week-24 guesses no better than chance despite more drowsiness on mirtazapine.

34% to 41% of urine results missing at weeks 12, 24 and 36, more dropout on mirtazapine (33% vs 22%); the primary analysis assumes missingness completely at random given time and arm. Imputing missing samples as positive reportedly preserved significance, but the estimate is only in an unread supplement.
Objective urine testing applied identically in both arms.

Primary and secondary outcomes registered before enrolment and unchanged, matching the paper; the analysis model is described as prespecified, with the protocol supplied as a supplement. Exploratory outcomes (depression, insomnia, abstinence) are reported alongside without adjustment.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A prospectively registered, well-concealed double-blind trial with an objective primary outcome whose analysis follows its registration. The concern is missing data: more than a third of urine results are missing at each assessment, dropout is higher on mirtazapine, and the primary analysis relies on missing-completely-at-random assumptions, with the conservative imputation result not shown in the article. The relative risks are also model-based divergences that are larger than the raw cross-sectional contrasts, partly because the mirtazapine arm started with more positive urines.

key_findings.finding: 120 participants randomized 60:60 (115 cisgender men, 5 transgender women who have sex with men) from 241 assessed; mean age 43.3; 51.7% HIV-positive; 80% urine-positive at baseline (85% mirtazapine, 75% placebo).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Participants; Table 1; Results › Methamphetamine use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome (intention to treat): RR of a methamphetamine-positive urine 0.67 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.87), P = .003, at 12 weeks; net RR 0.75 (0.56 to 1.00), P = .05, at 24 weeks; net RR 0.73 (0.57 to 0.96), P = .02, at 36 weeks (12 weeks after medication stopped).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Primary outcomes; Results › Methamphetamine use
key_findings.note: Model-based divergence of piecewise linear trends after accounting for the fitted baseline difference; the meaning of the 'net' 24- and 36-week estimates is defined only in footnotes (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Raw urine positivity among samples provided: week 12, 25 of 38 (66%) mirtazapine vs 32 of 41 (78%) placebo; week 24, 20 of 32 (63%) vs 29 of 39 (74%); week 36, 25 of 35 (71%) vs 37 of 42 (88%). Editors' calculation: risk differences -12.3 (95% CI -32.0 to 7.4), -11.9 (-33.5 to 9.8) and -16.7 (-34.6 to 1.2) percentage points; ratios of 0.84, 0.84 and 0.81.

Abstinence: end-of-study abstinence (no positive urine in the last 2 weeks) in 11 (18%) vs 5 (8%) at weeks 12 and 24 (OR 2.50, 0.80 to 7.61; P = .11) and 7 (12%) vs 3 (5%) at week 36 (OR 2.50, 0.62 to 10.20; P = .19); median beyond-threshold weeks of success 0 (IQR 0 to 0) in both arms at all points.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Number of beyond-threshold weeks of success

key_findings.finding: Missing urine results: 41 of 120 (34%) at week 12, 49 (41%) at week 24 and 43 (36%) at week 36, against 10%, 15% and 20% assumed; dropout 20 (33%) on mirtazapine vs 13 (22%) on placebo (P = .21).
key_findings.locator: Results › Methamphetamine use, 2nd paragraph; Retention and adherence

key_findings.finding: Adherence by WisePill dispenser was low and similar by arm: 38.5% vs 39.5% over weeks 2 to 12 (P = .77); over weeks 13 to 24 printed as 28.1% vs 38.5% (P = .59); self-reported 44.3% vs 46.1% and 38.8% vs 37.5%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 2; Results › Medication adherence
key_findings.note: The week-24 placebo values repeat the week-12 mirtazapine values exactly and are hard to reconcile with P = .59 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sexual risk (self-report): no differences at 12 weeks; at 24 weeks fewer male partners (RR 0.52, 0.27 to 0.97), fewer condomless anal sex episodes with serodiscordant partners (0.47, 0.23 to 0.97) and fewer condomless receptive episodes with serodiscordant partners (0.37, 0.14 to 0.93), all P = .04; partners with whom methamphetamine was used 0.54 (0.26 to 1.14) and anal sex with serodiscordant partners 0.53 (0.28 to 1.01) not significant; no differences at 36 weeks.

Depression and sleep: CES-D net 6.18 points lower on mirtazapine at 24 weeks (1.30 to 11.07; P = .01), not at 12 or 36 weeks; Athens Insomnia Scale 1.40 points lower at 24 weeks (0.07 to 2.74; P = .04); no differences in craving or dependence severity.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Craving, severity of dependence, depressive symptoms, and sleep

key_findings.finding: Safety: serious adverse events reported as nine, none judged drug-related; listed on mirtazapine: a death from unintentional opioid overdose and hospitalizations for deep venous thrombosis, congestive heart failure and soft-tissue infection; on placebo: shoulder injury, COPD, assault and lower respiratory infection. Fatigue or drowsiness 18 (30%) vs 6 (10%); weight gain 4 (7%) vs 1 (2%); hyperglycaemia 14 (23%) vs 11 (18%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: drowsiness risk difference 20 percentage points (6.1 to 33.9), Fisher's exact p = 0.011. Only eight serious events are itemized.

key_findings.finding: Registration NCT01888835, first submitted 25 June 2013 (before the August 2013 start); registered primary outcome (methamphetamine-positive urine tests at 12 and 24 weeks and sustained to 36 weeks) and secondary sexual-risk outcomes unchanged since registration; no results posted on the registry.
key_findings.page: ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT01888835 (current version and history)
key_findings.locator: Outcome Measures; Study Record History; Eligibility
key_findings.note: Read from the registry, not from the article, and not re-checked: neither reading of this card had access to ClinicalTrials.gov, so the registration date, the outcome history and the absence of posted results remain single-reader. The article prints only the registration number (Abstract, Trial Registration) and states that the analysis model was prespecified in the protocol, which is in a supplement that was not read. A reader with web access should confirm this finding at the registry.

reporting_issues.issue: Trial completion is given as 38 participants (48%) on mirtazapine and 42 (53%) on placebo, but 38 of 60 is 63% and 42 of 60 is 70% (the same counts are given correctly as 63% and 70% for week-36 visits).
reporting_issues.consequence: The completion percentages are wrong; retention to the final visit was 63% and 70%.

reporting_issues.issue: Week-24 visit completion is 43 of 60 (72%) in both arms but is reported with P = .28; identical proportions cannot give that P value.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error, probably a P value copied from another comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: WisePill adherence over weeks 13 to 24 is printed as 28.1% (SD 23.4) on mirtazapine versus 38.5% (SD 27.0) on placebo with P = .59; the placebo figures duplicate the mirtazapine figures for weeks 2 to 12, and a 10-point difference with these SDs would give P of roughly .03 to .06 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the adherence values is likely a copying error; the claim that adherence was similar by arm in the second period cannot be checked, and secondary sources quoting '28.1 to 39.5%' inherit the error.

reporting_issues.issue: The 24- and 36-week estimates are labelled 'net treatment effects' that account for differences from the beginning of each period, and the 36-week footnote describes weeks 25 to 36 as 'receiving treatment', although medication stopped at week 24.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the 24- and 36-week RRs are cumulative divergences from baseline or period-specific increments; editors' check: the raw positivity ratios at weeks 24 and 36 divided by the baseline ratio are about 0.74 and 0.72, close to the reported 0.75 and 0.73, which fits the cumulative reading. Claims about effects after stopping should state this uncertainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the 12-week Athens Insomnia Scale difference as 1.2 points lower with a 95% CI of 0.02 to 2.3 and P = .06, whereas Table 2 gives -1.15 (-2.33 to 0.02), an interval that includes zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign error in the text's interval; the 12-week sleep effect is not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Nine serious adverse events are reported but eight are itemized (four per arm).
reporting_issues.consequence: One serious event is unaccounted for in the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Eligibility in the paper differs from the registry: age 18 to 65 (registry 18 to 69), anal sex while using within 6 months (registry 3 months), five SSRIs permitted (registry excludes all antidepressants in the past 30 days).
reporting_issues.consequence: The registry was not updated to the criteria applied, or the paper describes them differently; four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs. Status of this item: the article side is confirmed by both readers (ages 18 to 65, anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months, five named SSRIs permitted, at Methods › Recruitment, and the four participants in the sensitivity analyses). The registry side is single-reader: ClinicalTrials.gov was not accessible in the second reading, so the 18-to-69 age range, the 3-month window and the antidepressant exclusion have not been re-checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points describe this trial and Colfax et al. (2011) as two independent randomized trials, although five authors, the site, the population, the counselling and the analysis model are shared.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two trials are a replication by the same team, not independent confirmation; claims should not count them as independent.

reporting_issues.issue: The wording of the 24-week result overstates its own interval. Results › Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph, puts weeks 12, 24 and 36 under one verb, saying the rate of methamphetamine-positive urine samples significantly declined by week 12 (RR 0.67, 0.51-0.87), week 24 (RR 0.75, 0.56-1.00) and week 36 (RR 0.73, 0.57-0.96); the abstract says mirtazapine resulted in reductions at 24 weeks. The 24-week interval reaches 1.00, and Table 2 gives P = .05 for it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any claim that mirtazapine lowered use at 24 weeks should print the interval, which is what makes the borderline result visible. The word significant cannot be carried over from this sentence for the 24-week estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: Visit completion is reported as a mean of 66% with an SD of 47%, while the arm figures are 69% (SD 32%) and 63% (SD 31%) (Results › Retention and Adherence, and the abstract). An SD of 47% is what a yes-or-no visit indicator with a mean of 0.66 gives, so the overall figure is computed over visits while the arm figures are computed over participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the overall SD is not comparable with the arm SDs and should not be quoted as participant-level variability in visit completion.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6990973 (all sections, Key Points, Tables 1 to 3 rendered as text, article notes with author contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, funding and role of funder, and reference list read; Figure 1 (CONSORT) and Figure 2 (urine positivity by week) are images and their values were not extracted; Supplement 1 (eTable, eFigure), Supplement 2 (protocol) and Supplement 3 not read). Registration, outcome and eligibility history additionally read from ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01888835.

disagreements.reviewer: missed: the Results and the abstract describe the 24-week effect as a significant decline or a reduction although its interval reaches 1.00 (P = .05); the card records the interval but not this wording, which matters for any claim that use was lowered at 24 weeks
disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue after reading both sentences in full: the Results sentence places all three time points under one verb, and the abstract uses reductions for 24 and 36 weeks after significantly declined for week 12. The interval and the P value are as the card already records them.

disagreements.reviewer: missed: overall weekly-visit completion is given as mean 66% with SD 47% while the arm SDs are 32% and 31%; 47% is the SD of a binary visit indicator at 66%, so the overall SD is on a different basis
disagreements.resolution: Added as a reporting issue. Checked in the source and recomputed: the square root of 0.66 times 0.34 is 0.474, which matches the printed 47%, so the reader's reading of the discrepancy is right.

disagreements.first_pass: funder, declared_conflicts and affiliations_note recorded from the article notes
disagreements.reviewer: missed: funding and conflict-of-interest details could not be checked, because the saved PMC text has no Article Information block; treat these card fields as single-reader
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; a sentence saying so is appended to funding.affiliations_note. The content is not disputed, only unverified by a second reader.

disagreements.reviewer: kept first-pass; key findings flagged: 1; reporting issues flagged: 1; risk of bias: agree
disagreements.resolution: Kept at first-pass after adjudication. Everything readable in the article was resolved, but two flagged items (key finding 9 and reporting issue 6) rest on the ClinicalTrials.gov record, which neither the second reader nor this adjudication could open, so they have had only one reader and the card does not meet the standard for ai-checked. It needs a targeted registry check by a reader with web access, after which the status can be raised. The risk-of-bias judgment (RoB 2, some concerns overall) is agreed, with the same caveat on the selection-of-reported-result domain, which rests partly on that registry history.
